Main.sentence: Counterterrorism (alternatively spelled: counter-terrorism ), also known as anti-terrorism , relates to the practices, ___E:military tactics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_tactics)___ , techniques, and strategies that governments, ___E:law enforcement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement)___ , businesses, and ___E:intelligence agencies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_agency)___ use to combat or eliminate ___E:terrorism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism)___ and ___E:violent extremism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violent_extremism)___ .

If an act of terrorism occurs as part of a broader ___E:insurgency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurgency)___ (and insurgency is included in the ___E:definition of terrorism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definition_of_terrorism)___ ) then counterterrorism may additionally employ ___E:counterinsurgency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterinsurgency)___ measures.

The ___E:United States Armed Forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Armed_Forces)___ uses the term " ___E:foreign internal defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_internal_defense)___ " for programs that support other countries' attempts to suppress insurgency, ___E:lawlessness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawlessness)___ , or ___E:subversion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subversion)___ , or to reduce the conditions under which threats to ___E:national security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_security)___ may develop.

The first counterterrorism body to be formed was the Special Irish Branch of the ___E:Metropolitan Police U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police)___ , later renamed the ___E:Special Branch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Branch_(Metropolitan_Police))___ after it expanded its scope beyond its original focus on ___E:Fenian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenian)___ terrorism.
Various ___E:law enforcement agencies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement_agency)___ established similar units in the United Kingdom and elsewhere.

The ___E:International Conference of Rome for the Social Defense Against Anarchists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Conference_of_Rome_for_the_Social_Defense_Against_Anarchists)___ has been identified as the first international conference against terrorism.

The first tactical counterterrorism unit was ___E:GSG 9 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GSG_9)___ of the ___E:West German U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_German)___ Federal Border Protection ( Bundesgrenzschutz ), which was later renamed the ___E:Federal Police U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Police_(Germany))___ ( Bundespolizei ) in 2005. GSG 9 was formed shortly after and in response to the Olympic ___E:Munich massacre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_massacre)___ of 1972.
Counterterrorist forces expanded with the perceived growing threat of terrorism in the late 20th century.
After the ___E:September 11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ , Western governments made counterterrorism efforts a priority.
This included more extensive collaboration with foreign governments, shifting tactics involving ___E:red teams U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_team)___ ,  and preventive measures.
Although terrorist attacks affecting Western countries generally receive a disproportionately large share of media attention,  most terrorism occurs in less developed countries.

Government responses to terrorism, in some cases, tend to lead to substantial unintended consequences,  [vague] such as what occurred in the above-mentioned Munich massacre. [further explanation needed]
Most counterterrorism strategies involve an increase in policing and domestic ___E:intelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_intelligence)___ gathering.
Central techniques include ___E:intercepting communications U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiretapping)___ and ___E:location tracking U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_system)___ .

New technology has expanded the range of ___E:military U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhunt_(military))___ and ___E:law enforcement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhunt_(law_enforcement))___ options for intelligence gathering.
Many countries increasingly employ ___E:facial recognition systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_recognition_system)___ in policing.

Domestic intelligence gathering is sometimes directed to specific ___E:ethnic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnicity)___ or religious groups, which are the sources of political conversy. ___E:Mass surveillance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_surveillance)___ of an entire population raises objections on ___E:civil liberties U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_liberties)___ grounds. ___E:Domestic terrorists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_terrorism)___ , especially ___E:lone wolves U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_wolf_attack)___ , are often harder to detect because of their citizenship or legal status and ability to stay under the radar.

To select the effective action when terrorism appears to be more of an isolated event, the appropriate government organizations need to understand the source, motivation, methods of preparation, and tactics of terrorist groups.
Good intelligence is at the heart of such preparation, as well as a political and social understanding of any grievances that might be solved.

Ideally, one gets information from inside the group, a very difficult challenge for ___E:human intelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_intelligence_(intelligence_gathering))___ operations because ___E:operational terrorist cells U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clandestine_cell_system)___ are often small, with all members known to one another, perhaps even related.

___E:Counterintelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterintelligence)___ is a great challenge with the security of cell-based systems, since the ideal, but the nearly impossible, goal is to obtain a ___E:clandestine source U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clandestine_human_intelligence)___ within the cell. Financial tracking can play a role, as a ___E:communications intercept U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signals_intelligence)___ .
However, both of these approaches need to be balanced against legitimate expectations of privacy.
In response to the growing legislation.

Since 1978 the UK's terrorism laws have been regularly reviewed by a security-cleared ___E:Independent Reviewer of Terrorism Legislation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Reviewer_of_Terrorism_Legislation)___ , whose often influential reports are submitted to Parliament and published in full.

One of the primary difficulties of implementing effective counterterrorist measures is the waning of civil liberties and individual privacy that such measures often entail, both for citizens of, and for those detained by states attempting to combat terror.
At times, measures designed to tighten security have been seen as ___E:abuses of power U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuses_of_power)___ or even violations of human rights.

Examples of these problems can include prolonged, incommunicado detention without judicial review or long periods of 'preventive detention';  risk of subjecting to torture during the transfer, return and extradition of people between or within countries; and the adoption of security measures that restrain the rights or freedoms of citizens and breach principles of non-discrimination.
Examples include:
Many argue that such violations of rights could exacerbate rather than counter the terrorist threat.
Human rights activists argue for the crucial role of human rights protection as an intrinsic part to fight against terrorism.

This suggests, as proponents of ___E:human security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_security)___ have long argued, that respecting human rights may indeed help us to incur security. ___E:Amnesty International U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International)___ included a section on confronting terrorism in the recommendations in the Madrid Agenda arising from the Madrid Summit on Democracy and Terrorism (Madrid March 8–11, 2005):
Democratic principles and values are essential tools in the fight against terrorism.
Any successful strategy for dealing with terrorism requires terrorists to be isolated.

Consequently, the preference must be to treat terrorism as criminal acts to be handled through existing systems of law enforcement and with full respect for human rights and the rule of law. We recommend: (1) taking effective measures to make impunity impossible either for acts of terrorism or for the abuse of human rights in counter-terrorism measures. (2) the incorporation of human rights laws in all anti-terrorism programs and policies of national governments as well as international bodies."

While international efforts to combat terrorism have focused on the need to enhance cooperation between states, proponents of human rights (as well as ___E:human security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_security)___ ) have suggested that more effort needs to be given to the effective inclusion of human rights protection as a crucial element in that cooperation.

They argue that international human rights obligations do not stop at borders, and a failure to respect human rights in one state may undermine its effectiveness in the global effort to cooperate to combat terrorism.
Some countries see preemptive attacks as a legitimate strategy.
This includes capturing, killing, or disabling suspected terrorists before they can mount an attack.
Israel, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Russia have taken this approach, while Western European states generally do not. [citation needed]

Another major method of preemptive neutralization is the ___E:interrogation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interrogation)___ of known or suspected terrorists to obtain information about specific plots, targets, the identity of other terrorists, whether or not the interrogation subjects himself is guilty of terrorist involvement.

Sometimes more extreme methods are used to increase ___E:suggestibility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suggestibility)___ , such as ___E:sleep deprivation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_deprivation)___ or drugs. [citation needed] Such methods may lead captives to offer false information in an attempt to stop the treatment, or due to the confusion caused by it. [citation needed] In 1978 the ___E:European Court of Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights)___ ruled in the ___E:Ireland v. United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_v._United_Kingdom_(1978))___ case that ___E:such methods U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_techniques)___ amounted to a practice of ___E:inhuman and degrading treatment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inhuman_or_degrading_treatment)___ , and that such practices were in breach of the ___E:European Convention on Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Convention_on_Human_Rights)___ Article 3 (art. 3). [citation needed]

The ___E:human security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_security)___ paradigm outlines a non-military approach that aims to address the enduring underlying inequalities which fuel terrorist activity.
Causal factors need to be delineated and measures implemented which allow equal access to resources and ___E:sustainability U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainability)___ for all people.
Such activities empower citizens, providing "freedom from fear" and "freedom from want". [citation needed]
This can take many forms, including the provision of clean drinking water, education, vaccination programs, provision of food and shelter and protection from violence, military or otherwise.

Successful human security campaigns have been characterized by the participation of a diverse group of actors, including governments, ___E:NGOs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGOs)___ , and citizens. [citation needed]
___E:Foreign internal defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_internal_defense)___ programs provide outside expert assistance to a threatened government.
FID can involve both non-military and military aspects of counterterrorism. [citation needed]
A 2017 study found that "governance and civil society aid is effective in dampening domestic terrorism, but this effect is only present if the recipient country is not experiencing a civil conflict."
Terrorism has often been used to justify ___E:military intervention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_intervention)___ in countries where terrorists are said to be based.

Similar justifications were used for the ___E:U.S. invasion of Afghanistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%932021))___ and the ___E:second Russian invasion of Chechnya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Chechen_War)___ .

Military intervention has not always been successful in stopping or preventing future terrorism, such as during the ___E:Malayan Emergency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayan_Emergency)___ , the ___E:Mau Mau uprising U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_uprising)___ , and most of the campaigns against the ___E:IRA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Republican_Army)___ during the ___E:Irish Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Civil_War)___ , the ___E:S-Plan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-Plan)___ , the ___E:Border Campaign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_campaign_(Irish_Republican_Army))___ , and ___E:the Troubles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles)___ in Northern Ireland.
Although military action can temporarily disrupt a terrorist group's operations temporarily, it sometimes does not end the threat completely.

Repression by the military in itself usually leads to short term victories, but tend to be unsuccessful in the long run (e.g., the French doctrine used in colonial ___E:Indochina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia)___ and ___E:Algeria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria)___  ), particularly if it is not accompanied by other measures.
However, new methods such as those taken in ___E:Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq)___ have yet to be seen as beneficial or ineffectual.
Whatever the target of terrorists, there are multiple ways of hardening the targets to prevent the terrorists from hitting their mark, or reducing the damage of attacks.

One method is to place ___E:hostile vehicle mitigation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hostile_vehicle_mitigation)___ to enforce protective standoff distance outside tall or politically sensitive buildings to prevent ___E:car bombings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_bomb)___ .
Another way to reduce the impact of attacks is to design buildings for rapid evacuation.
Aircraft cockpits are kept locked during flights and have reinforced doors, which only the pilots in the cabin are capable of opening.

UK ___E:railway stations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_stations)___ removed their garbage bins in response to the ___E:Provisional IRA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army)___ threat, as convenient locations for depositing bombs.
Scottish stations removed theirs after the ___E:7 July 2005 London Bombings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_July_2005_London_Bombings)___ as a precautionary measure.
The ___E:Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority)___ purchased bomb-resistant barriers after the September 11 attacks.

Due to frequent shelling of Israel's cities, towns, and settlements by ___E:artillery rockets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery_rocket)___ from the ___E:Gaza Strip U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip)___ (mainly by ___E:Hamas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas)___ , but also by other Palestinian factions) and ___E:Lebanon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon)___ (mainly by ___E:Hezbollah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hezbollah)___ ), Israel has developed several defensive measures against artillery, rockets, and missiles.

These include building a ___E:bomb shelter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomb_shelter)___ in every building and school, but also deploying ___E:active protection systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_protection_system)___ such as the ___E:Arrow ABM U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow_(missile_family))___ , ___E:Iron Dome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Dome)___ and ___E:David's Sling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David%27s_Sling)___ , which intercept the incoming threat in the air. ___E:Iron Dome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Dome)___ has successfully intercepted hundreds of ___E:Qassam rockets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qassam_rocket)___ and ___E:Grad rockets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BM-21_Grad)___ fired by Palestinians from the Gaza Strip.
A more sophisticated target-hardening approach must consider industrial and other critical industrial infrastructure that could be attacked.

Terrorists do not need to import chemical weapons if they can cause a major industrial accident such as the ___E:Bhopal disaster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhopal_disaster)___ or the ___E:Halifax Explosion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Explosion)___ .
Industrial chemicals in manufacturing, shipping, and storage thus require greater protection, and some efforts are in progress.
Equipping likely targets with containers of pig lard has been used to discourage attacks by suicide bombers.
The technique was apparently used on a limited scale by British authorities in the 1940s.
The approach stems from the idea that Muslims perpetrating the attack would not want to be "soiled" by the lard in the moment before dying.
The idea has been suggested more recently as a deterrent to suicide bombings in Israel.
However, the actual effectiveness of this tactic is likely limited.
A sympathetic Islamic scholar could issue a ___E:fatwa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatwa)___ proclaiming that a suicide bomber would not be polluted by the swine products.

For a threatened or completed terrorist attack, an ___E:Incident Command System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incident_Command_System)___ (ICS) may be invoked to control the various services that may need to be involved in the response.

ICS has varied levels of escalation, such as might be required for multiple incidents in a given area (e.g. ___E:2005 London bombings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_July_2005_London_bombings)___ or the ___E:2004 Madrid train bombings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Madrid_train_bombings)___ ), or all the way to a ___E:National Response Plan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Response_Plan)___ invocation if national-level resources are needed.
For example, a national response might be required for a nuclear, biological, radiological, or significant chemical attack.

___E:Fire departments U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_department)___ , perhaps supplemented by public works agencies, utility providers, and heavy construction contractors, are most apt to deal with the physical consequences of an attack.

Again under an incident command model, local police can isolate the incident area, reducing confusion, and specialized police units can conduct tactical operations against terrorists, often using specialized counterterrorist tactical units.
Bringing in such units will typically involve civil or military authority beyond the local level.

___E:Emergency medical services U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_medical_services)___ are capable of triaging, treating, and transporting the more severely affected individuals to hospitals, which typically have ___E:mass casualty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass-casualty_incident)___ and ___E:triage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triage)___ plans in place for terrorist attacks.

From the local to the national level, ___E:public health agencies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health_surveillance)___ may be designated to deal with identification or mitigation of possible biological attacks, including chemical or radiological contamination.
Many countries have dedicated counterterrorist units trained to handle terrorist threats.

Besides various ___E:security agencies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_agency)___ , there are ___E:police tactical units U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_tactical_unit)___ whose role is to directly engage terrorists and prevent terrorist attacks.
Such units perform both in preventive actions, hostage rescue, and responding to ongoing attacks.
Countries of all sizes can have highly trained counterterrorist teams.
Tactics, techniques, and procedures for ___E:manhunting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhunt_(military))___ are under constant development.

These units are specially trained in ___E:military tactics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_tactics)___ and are equipped for ___E:close-quarters combat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close-quarters_combat)___ , with emphasis on stealth and performing the mission with minimal casualties.

The units include assault teams, ___E:snipers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sniper)___ , ___E:EOD U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomb_disposal)___ experts, dog handlers, and intelligence officers.

Most of these measures deal with terrorist attacks that affect an area or threaten to do so, or are lengthy situations such as ___E:shootouts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shootout)___ and ___E:standoffs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_standoff)___ that allow the counterterrorist units to assemble and respond; it is harder to deal with shorter incidents such as assassinations, reprisal attacks, or bombings due to the short warning time and the quick exfiltration of the perpetrators.

The majority of counterterrorism operations at the tactical level are conducted by state, federal, and national law enforcement or ___E:intelligence agencies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_agency)___ .
In some countries, the military may be called in as a last resort.
For countries whose military is legally permitted to conduct domestic law enforcement operations, this is not an issue, and such counterterrorism operations are conducted by their military.

subsequently ___E:Mogadishu International Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mogadishu_International_Airport)___ , ___E:Somalia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_Democratic_Republic)___

March 30, the Manawan Police Academy in Lahore attack – 8 gunmen, 8 police personnel and 2 civilians killed, 95 people injured, 4 gunmen captured. [citation needed] Plaza Cinema Chowk attack – 16 police officers, an army officer and unknown number of civilians killed.
As many as 251 people injured. [citation needed]

The scope for counterterrorism systems is very large in physical terms and in other dimensions, such as type and degree of terrorist threats, political and diplomatic ramifications, and legal concerns.

Ideal counterterrorist systems use technology to enable persistent ___E:intelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence)___ , surveillance and reconnaissance missions, and potential actions.
Designing such a system-of-systems comprises a major technological project.

A particular design problem for counterterrorist systems is the uncertainty of the future: the threat of terrorism may increase, decrease or remain the same, the type of terrorism and location are difficult to predict, and there are technological uncertainties.

A potential solution is to incorporate ___E:engineering flexibility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexibility_(engineering))___ into system design, allowing for flexibility when new information arrives.
Flexibility can be incorporated in the design of a counter-terrorism system in the form of options that can be exercised in the future when new information is available.

While some countries with longstanding terrorism problems have law enforcement agencies primarily designed to prevent and respond to terror attacks,  in other nations, counterterrorism is a relatively more recent objective of law enforcement agencies.

Though some ___E:civil libertarians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_libertarianism)___ and ___E:criminal justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_justice)___ scholars have criticized efforts of law enforcement agencies to combat terrorism as futile and expensive  or as threats to civil liberties,  other scholars have analyzed the most important dimensions of the policing of terrorism as an important dimension of counter-terrorism, especially in the post-9/11 era, and have discussed how police view terrorism as a matter of crime control.
Such analyses highlight the civilian police role in counterterrorism next to the military model of a war on terror.

Pursuant to passage of the ___E:Homeland Security Act of 2002 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeland_Security_Act_of_2002)___ , federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies began to systemically reorganize.

Two primary federal agencies, the ___E:Department of Justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice)___ (DOJ) and the ___E:Department of Homeland Security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Homeland_Security)___ (DHS), house most of the federal agencies that are prepared to combat domestic and international terrorist attacks.

These include the ___E:Border Patrol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Border_Patrol)___ , the ___E:Secret Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secret_Service)___ , the ___E:Coast Guard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Coast_Guard)___ and the ___E:FBI U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI)___ .
Following suit from federal changes pursuant to 9/11, however, most state and local law enforcement agencies began to include a commitment to "fighting terrorism" in their mission statements.
Local agencies began to establish more patterned lines of communication with federal agencies.
Some scholars have doubted the ability of local police to help in the war on terror and suggest their limited manpower is still best utilized by engaging community and targeting street crimes.

While counter-terror measures (most notably heightened airport security, immigrant ___E:profiling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_profiling)___  and border patrol) have been adapted during the last decade, to enhance counter-terror in law enforcement, there have been remarkable limitations to assessing the actual utility/effectiveness of law enforcement practices that are ostensibly preventative.

Thus, while sweeping changes in counterterrorist rhetoric redefined most American post 9/11 law enforcement agencies in theory, it is hard to assess how well such hyperbole has translated into practice.

In ___E:intelligence-led policing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence-led_policing)___ (ILP) efforts, the most quantitatively amenable starting point for measuring the effectiveness of any policing strategy (i.e.: Neighborhood Watch, Gun Abatement, Foot Patrols, etc.) is usually to assess total financial costs against clearance rates or arrest rates.
Since terrorism is such a rare event phenomena,  measuring arrests or clearance rates would be a non-generalizable and ineffective way to test enforcement policy effectiveness.

Another methodological problem in assessing counterterrorism efforts in law enforcement hinges on finding operational measures for key concepts in the study of ___E:homeland security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeland_security)___ .

Both terrorism and homeland security are relatively new concepts for criminologists, and academicians have yet to agree on the matter of how to properly define these ideas in a way that is accessible.
Given the nature of operational counterterrorism tasks, national military organizations do not generally have dedicated units whose sole responsibility is the prosecution of these tasks.
Instead the counterterrorism function is an element of the role, allowing flexibility in their employment, with operations being undertaken in the domestic or international context.

In some cases the legal framework within which they operate prohibits military units conducting operations in the domestic arena; ___E:United States Department of Defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense)___ policy, based on the ___E:Posse Comitatus Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posse_Comitatus_Act)___ , forbids domestic counterterrorism operations by the U.S. military.
Units allocated some operational counterterrorism tasks are frequently ___E:special forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_forces)___ or similar assets.

In cases where military organisations do operate in the domestic context, some form of formal handover from the law enforcement community is regularly required, to ensure adherence to the legislative framework and limitations.

For instance, during the 1980 ___E:Iranian Embassy siege U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Embassy_siege)___ , the ___E:Metropolitan Police U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police)___ formally turned responsibility over to the ___E:British Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army)___ 's ___E:Special Air Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Air_Service)___ when the situation went beyond police capabilities.
